script.opening: "Cheers for seeing me on video — saves the awkwardness. Look, my piles are back, I’ve been bleeding when I go, so I just need some of that cream and a prescription for it really. Last time it sorted itself. I don’t want a load of fuss or examinations if I can help it — can you just send something to the chemist so I can get back on the road?"

facts.text: If properly explored: bleeding ~8 weeks, sometimes DARKER and MIXED IN with the stool (not just bright-red on the paper as with piles), occurring most times he opens his bowels. He glosses this as "the piles".

On direct questioning: looser stools and going more frequently for ~2 months (change in bowel habit), and unintentional weight loss of ~½ stone he’s put down to "being busy / not eating much on the road". Possibly more tired than usual. These transform the picture.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the "just piles" is fear-driven denial: his father died of bowel cancer at 60, he watched it, and he is privately terrified the same is happening to him. Booking a VIDEO appointment and pushing for cream is a way to avoid the examination and the answer he dreads. He half-knows the bleeding isn’t like last time.

If reached gently: he’s noticed the change for weeks but kept rebooking "cream" rather than face it; can’t afford time off (self-employed, sole earner); and is frightened of leaving his kids without a dad like his father left him.

Officially: cream and to be left alone. What he needs: recognition that rectal bleeding with change in bowel habit and weight loss at 52 is a suspected colorectal cancer picture — FIT (NICE HTG690) and a face-to-face examination, with a suspected cancer pathway referral if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g (NICE NG12), delivered so he accepts it despite his fear, with the bereavement-driven terror met honestly.

ice.ideas: It’s just his old haemorrhoids flaring; cream will fix it like before.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his father died of bowel cancer at 60; he is terrified the same is happening and is using "piles/cream" and a video booking to avoid examination and the answer he dreads.
ice.expectations: A prescription for haemorrhoid cream and no examination. What he actually needs: FIT, examination, and an urgent colorectal suspected cancer pathway referral with the bereavement fear addressed.

cues: "Just send the cream, no examination" — minimising and avoidance of a red-flag symptom; the fear is underneath.
Blood mixed IN with stool + change in bowel habit + weight loss — not a piles story; the suspected cancer pathway picture.
Father died of bowel cancer — the dread driving the denial; surface it gently.

checkpoints.text: Does NOT accept the "just piles" self-diagnosis or prescribe cream blindly: recognises that bleeding mixed with stool, a change in bowel habit and unintentional weight loss are RED FLAGS that override a haemorrhoid label, especially at 52

Acts on the NICE NG12 / FIT pathway: offers quantitative faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) — NICE HTG690: change in bowel habit, or aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding or weight loss; he qualifies three ways — and refers on a colorectal suspected cancer pathway if FIT is positive (≥10 µg Hb/g); if FIT is below 10 but strong clinical concern persists, does not delay referral (NICE HTG690); refers on examination findings without FIT if there is a rectal mass, unexplained anal mass or anal ulceration; restates the threshold, tagged NICE NG12

Insists on appropriate EXAMINATION (abdominal exam and digital rectal examination, inspection for an obvious anal cause) rather than skipping it because he booked video — explaining why, and handling his reluctance with dignity

Checks for anaemia and weights the FAMILY HISTORY accurately: bloods (FBC and ferritin — iron-deficiency anaemia is itself an indication for FIT under NICE NG12, and BSG 2021 advises lower and upper GI investigation for iron deficiency anaemia in men), and recognises that one first-degree relative diagnosed at 60 does NOT reach the BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG (2019) moderate-risk bar (one first-degree relative under 50, or two at any age) — it raises the emotional stakes, but his symptoms drive the referral

Recognises what would escalate further (significant anaemia, abdominal/rectal mass, obstructive symptoms) and does not let "piles" defer the assessment; does not falsely reassure even if external piles are present (they can coexist with cancer)

Hears the denial as fear and surfaces the father’s bowel cancer gently; does not collude with "it’s just piles" nor frighten him into disengagement; balances honesty with the fact most rectal bleeding is benign
Accommodates the examination reluctance (chaperone, control, explanation) and the practical barriers (self-employed, time off), so he accepts the pathway

Safety-nets and follows up: explains FIT and the suspected cancer pathway timeframe (NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard: cancer diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral) and what to expect (colonoscopy or CT colonography), helps him return the FIT sample, what to do if heavier bleeding/obstruction, ensures he attends, documents, and arranges to follow up the result — does not leave a frightened man with a tube of cream

worked.txt: "I’m glad you came — and I want to be straight rather than just send cream, because that would let you down. What you’re describing isn’t quite a simple piles story: blood mixed in with the motion, your bowels looser and more often, and some weight dropping off. Those together always need checking properly, whatever the cause turns out to be."

"Here’s the plan. There’s a simple stool test called FIT that looks for hidden blood. With your symptoms, if it shows blood above the referral level — or if I find anything when I examine you — the right thing is an urgent referral to the bowel specialists, usually for a camera test, with the aim of having cancer ruled in or out within 28 days. The NICE suspected cancer guideline, NICE NG12, is clear on this, and even if the test is low I won’t just drop it while you still have symptoms. It is NOT me saying it’s cancer; it’s me making sure, fast."

"I do need to examine your tummy and back passage in person too — I know that’s the bit you hoped to dodge, and I’ll make it quick, with a chaperone, and stop the moment you say. Even if you DO have piles, piles can sit alongside something else, so finding them wouldn’t let me stop looking."

"Can I gently say — you mentioned your dad. Losing him to bowel cancer at sixty, and now bleeding yourself, I’d be amazed if that thought hadn’t been keeping you up. Is that part of why ‘piles and cream’ felt easier than coming in? … Thank you for telling me. That fear is exactly why we look properly now, so you’re not carrying it in the dark."

"Two honest things at once: most rectal bleeding turns out to be something benign, and I’m not predicting the worst. And — because of your symptoms and your dad — we don’t guess, we check. Both are true. Getting the all-clear quickly is worth far more than a tube of cream."

"I know time off the road is money, so I’ll help make this work — the FIT today, bloods, and the referral. If you get heavy bleeding, severe tummy pain, or can’t pass anything, that’s urgent, go to A&E. I’ll chase your results and we’ll go through them together. You came for cream; what I’m doing is making sure your kids keep their dad. That’s the deal."

f.learning: Rectal bleeding that is mixed with stool, accompanied by a change in bowel habit (looser, more frequent) and unintentional weight loss at age 52 is a lower-GI suspected cancer pathway picture — NOT a haemorrhoid story to be treated blindly with cream. The NICE NG12/FIT pathway applies: offer quantitative FIT (NICE HTG690) and refer on a colorectal suspected cancer pathway if FIT is positive (≥10 µg Hb/g); with this symptom cluster, a FIT below 10 does not end the matter if strong concern persists (NICE HTG690). His father’s cancer at 60 is not in itself a moderate-risk family history (BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG 2019) — the symptoms drive the referral. The suspected cancer pathway aims for a diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days (NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard). Examination (abdominal + DRE, anal inspection) and an FBC and ferritin for iron-deficiency anaemia (itself a FIT indication) are essential — and must not be skipped because the patient booked a video; visible piles can coexist with cancer and never excuse stopping the work-up. The examinable hidden agenda is bereavement-driven denial: his father died of bowel cancer, and "piles/cream/video" is avoidance of the examination and answer he dreads. Surface the fear gently, balance honesty with the fact most bleeding is benign, accommodate the examination reluctance and his practical barriers, and complete the FIT and suspected cancer pathway with follow-up.

knowledge.guideline: NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) — FIT in primary care · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BSG iron deficiency anaemia guideline (2021) · BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG hereditary colorectal cancer guideline (2019)
knowledge.summary: Eight weeks of blood mixed with the stool, looser and more frequent motions and unintended weight loss at 52 is a suspected colorectal cancer picture until tested, not a piles flare. Offer FIT, examine in person and check an FBC; FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g means a suspected cancer pathway referral.

points.t: NICE HTG690: offer quantitative FIT to guide referral in adults with a change in bowel habit, or aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss. Gary meets it three ways. A previous negative screening FIT does not stop a symptomatic FIT being offered.

NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for colorectal cancer if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g faeces. A rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration does not need FIT first — refer on examination findings.

points.h: A low FIT does not close the case
points.t: NICE HTG690: if FIT is below 10 µg Hb/g, safety-net and do not delay referral to an appropriate secondary care pathway when there is strong clinical concern from ongoing unexplained symptoms. Help people who may struggle to return the sample.

Haemorrhoids cause bright-red blood on the paper or dripping into the pan. They do not explain dark blood mixed with the motion, eight weeks of altered habit or weight loss, and visible piles can sit alongside a cancer. Anchoring on a known benign label is a classic cause of delay.

Abdominal examination, anal inspection and digital rectal examination are part of the assessment and need a face-to-face appointment. Check FBC and ferritin: BSG (2021) advises lower and upper GI investigation for iron deficiency anaemia in men.

BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG (2019): one first-degree relative diagnosed under 50, or two first-degree relatives at any age, is moderate risk with a one-off colonoscopy at 55. A father diagnosed at 60 alone does not reach that bar — it raises the emotional stakes here, but his symptoms are what drive the referral.

Suspected cancer pathway referral (NG12). The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023) aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral. Usually colonoscopy or CT colonography.

dg.d: Open question on the bleeding rather than writing the cream; confirmed privacy on video; let him give his own account first.
Self-employed lorry driver and sole earner, children at home, what time off means financially, and the video booking as avoidance.
Face-to-face abdominal examination, anal inspection and DRE with chaperone; FIT; FBC and ferritin.
Colorectal cancer, haemorrhoids, fissure, inflammatory bowel disease; blood mixed in the stool and altered habit weighed against a piles pattern.
Asked about weight loss, tiredness, tenesmus, pain, heavy bleeding and faintness; knows a rectal mass means referral without waiting for FIT.
States a suspected colorectal cancer picture needing FIT and likely urgent referral, not a haemorrhoid flare, in plain language.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: FIT with the NICE NG12 threshold (at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway), examination and bloods booked around his work; no cream as a substitute.
Iron deficiency acted on if found; family history recorded accurately; practical and financial barriers addressed.
Named A&E triggers, dated examination, GP owns the FIT result and referral, teach-back of the plan.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: “It’s not like last time”, the father’s bowel cancer, and “no examinations” — each picked up and explored rather than passed over.
Idea (piles flare), the hidden concern (the same cancer as his father; leaving his children), and his expectation of cream with no examination.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — his father died of bowel cancer at 60; he is terrified the same is happening and is using "piles/cream" and a video booking to avoid examination and the answer he dreads — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Underwood, I’m Dr Lee. Can I just check you’re somewhere private where you can talk freely? … Great. I can see you’ve asked about some cream for piles — tell me what’s been going on.
model.why: Confirms privacy on video and opens with his story, not the prescription

model.text: Yeah, the piles are back. I’m bleeding when I go. Last time it sorted itself, so if you can send some cream to the chemist I’ll get back on the road. Don’t want a load of fuss or examinations.
Fair enough — I’ll keep this as quick as I can. I do want to understand the bleeding properly first so I give you the right thing, not just a thing. Then we’ll agree a plan. Is that okay?
model.why: Sets an agenda without agreeing to the cream in advance

model.text: Go on then.
When you say bleeding — how long has it been going on, and what does the blood look like? Is it bright red on the paper, or is it mixed in with the motion itself?
model.why: Characterises the bleeding — the single most discriminating question

model.text: About eight weeks. Mostly every time I go. Sometimes it’s darker… sort of mixed in. It’s not really like last time, if I’m honest.
Thank you, that’s really helpful. And have your bowels themselves changed at all — looser, more often, or harder to go?
model.why: Asks directly about change in bowel habit

model.text: Looser, yeah. Going more often, for a couple of months. I put it down to eating rubbish on the road.
Any weight loss you haven’t been trying for, or feeling more tired than usual? Any tummy pain, or feeling you haven’t finished after you’ve been?
model.why: Screens for weight loss, anaemia symptoms and tenesmus

model.text: Maybe half a stone off. I’ve been busy, not eating much. Bit more tired. No real pain.
And any heavy bleeding — clots, or feeling faint or dizzy when it happens?
model.why: Excludes a same-day bleed before planning a routine-urgent pathway

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Is there anyone in the family who’s had bowel problems?
My dad. Bowel cancer. He was sixty.
I’m sorry — that must have been a hard thing to go through. Can I ask gently, with your dad in mind, what’s been going through your head these last few weeks?
model.why: Picks up the bereavement cue and opens the hidden fear

model.text: …I watched him go downhill. I’ve got kids. I keep telling myself it’s piles because if it isn’t, I don’t know what I’d do. That’s why I booked a video, if I’m honest.

Thank you for telling me that — it takes a lot to say. It makes complete sense that ‘piles and some cream’ felt easier to ask for. I’d rather we face it together than you carry it on your own in the cab.
model.why: Validates the avoidance as fear without colluding with it

model.text: So let me be straight with you. Blood mixed in with the motion, looser bowels for two months and weight coming off — together, at 52, that isn’t a simple piles story, and cream wouldn’t be the right answer. It needs checking properly and quickly.
model.why: Declines the self-diagnosis and names the red-flag cluster in plain words

model.text: So you think it’s cancer.
I’m not saying that. Most bleeding from the back passage turns out to be something benign. But with your symptoms we don’t guess — we check. Both of those are true at the same time.

There are three parts. A simple stool test called FIT, which measures tiny amounts of blood — if it’s above a set level, national guidance says you go on the urgent suspected cancer pathway to the bowel team, usually for a camera test. A blood count, to check for anaemia. And I need to examine your tummy and back passage in person — even if I find piles, piles can sit alongside something else.
model.why: FIT with the NICE NG12 threshold, FBC and face-to-face examination

model.text: The examination’s the bit I was dodging.
I know. It takes a minute or two, you can have a chaperone, and I’ll stop the moment you ask. And if I felt anything on examination, I’d refer you straight away without waiting for the stool test.
model.why: Gives him control over the examination and explains its purpose

model.text: What would make this workable for you, with the driving and the work?
model.why: Invites his practical barriers into the plan

model.text: I’m self-employed. No work, no money. I can’t be off for weeks.

Then let’s be efficient. Could you come in today or tomorrow, early or late, for the examination and bloods, and pick up the FIT kit at the same visit? If the hospital does a camera test, it’s usually one morning, and they’ll give you the date in advance so you can plan your runs.
model.why: Tailors timing to a self-employed driver so the plan actually happens

model.text: Tomorrow first thing I could do.

Good. Meanwhile — if you get heavy bleeding, clots, feel faint, get bad tummy pain or can’t pass anything, go to A&E. I’ll check the FIT result myself as soon as it’s back and ring you, and if it meets the level I’ll send the referral that day.
model.why: Specific safety-net and a named owner for the result

model.text: Just so I know I’ve explained it well — what will you say at home about today?
That it might not be piles, that I’m getting a stool test and bloods, you’re examining me tomorrow, and if the test is up I get the camera quick. And that it’s probably nothing, but we’re checking.
That’s exactly it. You did the right thing booking in, even if it was for cream. See you tomorrow.

social.t: Time off the road is lost income. Plan appointments at the edges of his day and give dates early so he can schedule runs; this is what turns a referral into attendance.
Watching his father die of bowel cancer drives the minimising and the remote booking. Naming it kindly, and framing checking as protecting his children, is what brings him in.

legal.t: If he has sedation for colonoscopy he must not drive home and will be told by the unit how long to avoid driving afterwards — relevant to a lorry driver planning work. Investigation itself is not something he needs to notify DVLA about.

legal.h: Income if he needs time off
legal.t: Self-employed people cannot get Statutory Sick Pay; if longer time off is needed later, New Style ESA or Universal Credit may apply and need a fit note.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): if a remote consultation cannot meet the patient’s needs safely, arrange to see them in person. An examination that is needed is not skipped because of the booking type.
GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain why the examination is needed, offer a chaperone, get consent, and stop if asked. Document the offer and the outcome.
The requesting clinician owns the FIT result. Practice systems should track suspected cancer referrals and confirm the appointment happens.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Macmillan Cancer Support for information while he waits; the NHS Bowel Cancer Screening Programme for future home kits once this episode is settled.

redFlags: Blood mixed with the stool rather than only on the paper
Change in bowel habit — looser and more frequent for about two months
Unintended weight loss and tiredness (possible anaemia); ask about heavy bleeding, faintness, pain and obstruction
psychosocial: Self-employed lorry driver and sole earner — time off means lost income
Children at home; the fear of leaving them as his father left him
Booked a video and asked for cream to avoid being examined
ice: Idea: “It’s my old piles again — cream sorted it last time”
Concern: his father died of bowel cancer at 60 and he dreads the same
Expectation: a prescription and no examination

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest that this is not a piles picture: “Blood mixed in with the motion, looser bowels for two months and weight loss at 52 need checking for a bowel cause, including cancer — most people turn out fine, but we check rather than guess.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Piles usually give bright blood on the paper and nothing else. What you’re describing is more than that — like a warning light that could be something minor, but we need to lift the bonnet and look rather than just put tape over it.”

management.reflectIce: “You watched your dad go through this, and you’ve got kids of your own — no wonder cream felt easier to ask for. Getting a quick, clear answer is the best thing you can do for them.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around a self-employed driver: early or late appointment for the examination and bloods, FIT kit at the same visit, hospital dates given in advance so he can plan runs.
sharedPlan: FIT now; NICE NG12: at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway colorectal referral
Face-to-face abdominal examination, anal inspection and DRE with chaperone; refer without waiting for FIT if a mass is found
FBC and ferritin; if FIT is low but symptoms persist and concern is strong, refer anyway (NICE HTG690)
safetyNet: Heavy bleeding, clots, faintness, severe pain or inability to pass anything → A&E
GP rings with the FIT result and sends any referral the same day; confirm the hospital appointment is received

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by accepting the patient’s label. The history is easy to take if you ask the right two questions; the marks are lost when the cream goes out, the examination is skipped because the booking was remote, or the father’s death is never heard.

items.fail: Prescribing haemorrhoid cream because he has had piles before and asked for it.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Change in bowel habit and rectal bleeding at 50+ meet NICE HTG690 for FIT; a known benign diagnosis does not explain blood in the stool, altered habit and weight loss.
items.fix: Ask the discriminating questions — blood on the paper or mixed in, bowel habit, weight — then say plainly that cream is not the answer and why.

items.fail: Referring on symptoms alone without FIT, or quoting the old symptom-only suspected cancer referral criteria.
items.why: NICE NG12 makes FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g the referral trigger for most colorectal presentations; examiners expect the current pathway and the threshold stated.
items.fix: “The stool test decides the urgent referral — above 10 and you’re on the suspected cancer pathway. If I feel a lump on examination, I refer straight away.”

items.fail: Skipping the examination because the consultation is by video.
items.why: A rectal mass changes the pathway immediately, and GMC guidance expects an in-person assessment when remote care cannot meet the need.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face examination with a chaperone within a day or two, and explain exactly why it matters.

items.fail: Hearing “my dad had bowel cancer” and moving straight on to the plan.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The father’s death is the hidden agenda and the reason he is avoiding examination.
items.fix: Pause: “With your dad in mind, what’s been going through your head?” Then use his answer to shape the plan.

items.fail: Frightening him with “this could well be cancer” or overstating his inherited risk.
items.why: Catastrophising in a man already avoiding care risks disengagement; a single first-degree relative at 60 does not meet moderate-risk criteria (BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG 2019).
items.fix: Hold both truths: most bleeding is benign, and with these symptoms we check quickly.

items.fail: Ignoring the self-employed driver’s real constraints and offering a mid-morning slot next week.
items.why: A plan that does not fit his life will not happen — examiners mark whether the plan is tailored to the patient.
items.fix: Offer an early or late slot, FIT kit and bloods at the same visit, and hospital dates in advance.

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll let you know the results” and no named safety-net.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no owner for the result are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: “Heavy bleeding, faintness, bad pain or can’t pass anything — A&E. I’ll ring you with the FIT result myself.” Then teach-back.

Duration, blood on the paper or mixed in, bowel habit, weight, tiredness, pain, heavy bleeding. Family history — the father will surface.

Not a piles story. FIT (NICE NG12: at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway), FBC, face-to-face exam with chaperone. Fit it around his driving.
A&E triggers in plain words. GP owns the FIT result. Teach-back: “What will you say at home?”

wordPics.fail: Prescribes haemorrhoid cream on the video; never asks whether the blood is mixed in or about bowel habit and weight; skips examination because he booked remotely; never learns about the father; vague “come back if it doesn’t settle”.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the red-flag cluster; arranges FIT, FBC and a face-to-face examination; states the FIT threshold for referral; acknowledges his worry; gives a basic safety-net and follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: surfaces the father’s death and the avoidance behind the video booking with warmth; balances ‘most bleeding is benign’ with ‘we check, not guess’; gives him control over the examination; builds the plan around a self-employed driver’s day; owns the result; teach-back confirms he will attend.

avoid.instead: “Blood mixed in with the motion, looser bowels and weight loss isn’t a piles pattern. Cream wouldn’t be the right answer — let’s check properly.”
avoid.why: Accepting the self-label for a red-flag cluster is the core Tasks fail in this station.

avoid.dont: “Because your dad had bowel cancer, you’re at high risk of getting it too.”
avoid.instead: “With your symptoms, and knowing what happened to your dad, I want us to get a clear answer quickly.”
avoid.why: Overstates inherited risk and frightens a man already close to disengaging; the symptoms drive the referral.

avoid.dont: “I can’t do anything until I’ve examined you.”

avoid.why: A remote booking still allows action today; stalling wastes the consultation and his trust.

SCA_MODELS.why: Sets an agenda without agreeing to the cream in advance

SCA_MODELS.text: Go on then.
When you say bleeding — how long has it been going on, and what does the blood look like? Is it bright red on the paper, or is it mixed in with the motion itself?
SCA_MODELS.why: Characterises the bleeding — the single most discriminating question

SCA_MODELS.text: About eight weeks. Mostly every time I go. Sometimes it’s darker… sort of mixed in. It’s not really like last time, if I’m honest.
Thank you, that’s really helpful. And have your bowels themselves changed at all — looser, more often, or harder to go?
SCA_MODELS.why: Asks directly about change in bowel habit

SCA_MODELS.text: Looser, yeah. Going more often, for a couple of months. I put it down to eating rubbish on the road.
Any weight loss you haven’t been trying for, or feeling more tired than usual? Any tummy pain, or feeling you haven’t finished after you’ve been?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for weight loss, anaemia symptoms and tenesmus

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe half a stone off. I’ve been busy, not eating much. Bit more tired. No real pain.
And any heavy bleeding — clots, or feeling faint or dizzy when it happens?
SCA_MODELS.why: Excludes a same-day bleed before planning a routine-urgent pathway

SCA_MODELS.text: No, nothing like that.
Is there anyone in the family who’s had bowel problems?
My dad. Bowel cancer. He was sixty.
I’m sorry — that must have been a hard thing to go through. Can I ask gently, with your dad in mind, what’s been going through your head these last few weeks?
SCA_MODELS.why: Picks up the bereavement cue and opens the hidden fear

SCA_MODELS.text: …I watched him go downhill. I’ve got kids. I keep telling myself it’s piles because if it isn’t, I don’t know what I’d do. That’s why I booked a video, if I’m honest.

Thank you for telling me that — it takes a lot to say. It makes complete sense that ‘piles and some cream’ felt easier to ask for. I’d rather we face it together than you carry it on your own in the cab.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates the avoidance as fear without colluding with it

SCA_MODELS.text: So let me be straight with you. Blood mixed in with the motion, looser bowels for two months and weight coming off — together, at 52, that isn’t a simple piles story, and cream wouldn’t be the right answer. It needs checking properly and quickly.
SCA_MODELS.why: Declines the self-diagnosis and names the red-flag cluster in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: So you think it’s cancer.
I’m not saying that. Most bleeding from the back passage turns out to be something benign. But with your symptoms we don’t guess — we check. Both of those are true at the same time.

There are three parts. A simple stool test called FIT, which measures tiny amounts of blood — if it’s above a set level, national guidance says you go on the urgent suspected cancer pathway to the bowel team, usually for a camera test. A blood count, to check for anaemia. And I need to examine your tummy and back passage in person — even if I find piles, piles can sit alongside something else.
SCA_MODELS.why: FIT with the NICE NG12 threshold, FBC and face-to-face examination

SCA_MODELS.text: The examination’s the bit I was dodging.
I know. It takes a minute or two, you can have a chaperone, and I’ll stop the moment you ask. And if I felt anything on examination, I’d refer you straight away without waiting for the stool test.
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives him control over the examination and explains its purpose

SCA_MODELS.text: What would make this workable for you, with the driving and the work?
SCA_MODELS.why: Invites his practical barriers into the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: I’m self-employed. No work, no money. I can’t be off for weeks.

Then let’s be efficient. Could you come in today or tomorrow, early or late, for the examination and bloods, and pick up the FIT kit at the same visit? If the hospital does a camera test, it’s usually one morning, and they’ll give you the date in advance so you can plan your runs.
SCA_MODELS.why: Tailors timing to a self-employed driver so the plan actually happens

SCA_MODELS.text: Tomorrow first thing I could do.

Good. Meanwhile — if you get heavy bleeding, clots, feel faint, get bad tummy pain or can’t pass anything, go to A&E. I’ll check the FIT result myself as soon as it’s back and ring you, and if it meets the level I’ll send the referral that day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and a named owner for the result

SCA_MODELS.text: Just so I know I’ve explained it well — what will you say at home about today?
That it might not be piles, that I’m getting a stool test and bloods, you’re examining me tomorrow, and if the test is up I get the camera quick. And that it’s probably nothing, but we’re checking.
That’s exactly it. You did the right thing booking in, even if it was for cream. See you tomorrow.

SCA_STEM.name: Gary Underwood
pmh: Small external haemorrhoids noted some years ago
SCA_STEM.recent: Booked a video appointment online, reason given as “haemorrhoid cream”. Occupation: lorry driver. BMI 28. No FBC or FIT on record. Family history on file: father — bowel cancer, died aged 60.
SCA_STEM.reason: Requesting a prescription for haemorrhoid cream.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) — FIT in primary care · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BSG iron deficiency anaemia guideline (2021) · BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG hereditary colorectal cancer guideline (2019)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Eight weeks of blood mixed with the stool, looser and more frequent motions and unintended weight loss at 52 is a suspected colorectal cancer picture until tested, not a piles flare. Offer FIT, examine in person and check an FBC; FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g means a suspected cancer pathway referral.

points.t: NICE HTG690: offer quantitative FIT to guide referral in adults with a change in bowel habit, or aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss. Gary meets it three ways. A previous negative screening FIT does not stop a symptomatic FIT being offered.

NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for colorectal cancer if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g faeces. A rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration does not need FIT first — refer on examination findings.

points.h: A low FIT does not close the case
points.t: NICE HTG690: if FIT is below 10 µg Hb/g, safety-net and do not delay referral to an appropriate secondary care pathway when there is strong clinical concern from ongoing unexplained symptoms. Help people who may struggle to return the sample.

Haemorrhoids cause bright-red blood on the paper or dripping into the pan. They do not explain dark blood mixed with the motion, eight weeks of altered habit or weight loss, and visible piles can sit alongside a cancer. Anchoring on a known benign label is a classic cause of delay.

Abdominal examination, anal inspection and digital rectal examination are part of the assessment and need a face-to-face appointment. Check FBC and ferritin: BSG (2021) advises lower and upper GI investigation for iron deficiency anaemia in men.

BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG (2019): one first-degree relative diagnosed under 50, or two first-degree relatives at any age, is moderate risk with a one-off colonoscopy at 55. A father diagnosed at 60 alone does not reach that bar — it raises the emotional stakes here, but his symptoms are what drive the referral.

Suspected cancer pathway referral (NG12). The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023) aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral. Usually colonoscopy or CT colonography.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question on the bleeding rather than writing the cream; confirmed privacy on video; let him give his own account first.
Self-employed lorry driver and sole earner, children at home, what time off means financially, and the video booking as avoidance.
“It’s not like last time”, the father’s bowel cancer, and “no examinations” — each picked up and explored rather than passed over.
Idea (piles flare), the hidden concern (the same cancer as his father; leaving his children), and his expectation of cream with no examination.
Face-to-face abdominal examination, anal inspection and DRE with chaperone; FIT; FBC and ferritin.
Colorectal cancer, haemorrhoids, fissure, inflammatory bowel disease; blood mixed in the stool and altered habit weighed against a piles pattern.
Asked about weight loss, tiredness, tenesmus, pain, heavy bleeding and faintness; knows a rectal mass means referral without waiting for FIT.
States a suspected colorectal cancer picture needing FIT and likely urgent referral, not a haemorrhoid flare, in plain language.
FIT with the NICE NG12 threshold (at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway), examination and bloods booked around his work; no cream as a substitute.
Iron deficiency acted on if found; family history recorded accurately; practical and financial barriers addressed.
Named A&E triggers, dated examination, GP owns the FIT result and referral, teach-back of the plan.

social.t: Time off the road is lost income. Plan appointments at the edges of his day and give dates early so he can schedule runs; this is what turns a referral into attendance.
Watching his father die of bowel cancer drives the minimising and the remote booking. Naming it kindly, and framing checking as protecting his children, is what brings him in.

legal.t: If he has sedation for colonoscopy he must not drive home and will be told by the unit how long to avoid driving afterwards — relevant to a lorry driver planning work. Investigation itself is not something he needs to notify DVLA about.

legal.h: Income if he needs time off
legal.t: Self-employed people cannot get Statutory Sick Pay; if longer time off is needed later, New Style ESA or Universal Credit may apply and need a fit note.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): if a remote consultation cannot meet the patient’s needs safely, arrange to see them in person. An examination that is needed is not skipped because of the booking type.
GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain why the examination is needed, offer a chaperone, get consent, and stop if asked. Document the offer and the outcome.
The requesting clinician owns the FIT result. Practice systems should track suspected cancer referrals and confirm the appointment happens.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Macmillan Cancer Support for information while he waits; the NHS Bowel Cancer Screening Programme for future home kits once this episode is settled.

redFlags: Blood mixed with the stool rather than only on the paper
Change in bowel habit — looser and more frequent for about two months
Unintended weight loss and tiredness (possible anaemia); ask about heavy bleeding, faintness, pain and obstruction
psychosocial: Self-employed lorry driver and sole earner — time off means lost income
Children at home; the fear of leaving them as his father left him
Booked a video and asked for cream to avoid being examined
ice: Idea: “It’s my old piles again — cream sorted it last time”
Concern: his father died of bowel cancer at 60 and he dreads the same
Expectation: a prescription and no examination

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest that this is not a piles picture: “Blood mixed in with the motion, looser bowels for two months and weight loss at 52 need checking for a bowel cause, including cancer — most people turn out fine, but we check rather than guess.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Piles usually give bright blood on the paper and nothing else. What you’re describing is more than that — like a warning light that could be something minor, but we need to lift the bonnet and look rather than just put tape over it.”

management.reflectIce: “You watched your dad go through this, and you’ve got kids of your own — no wonder cream felt easier to ask for. Getting a quick, clear answer is the best thing you can do for them.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around a self-employed driver: early or late appointment for the examination and bloods, FIT kit at the same visit, hospital dates given in advance so he can plan runs.
sharedPlan: FIT now; NICE NG12: at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway colorectal referral
Face-to-face abdominal examination, anal inspection and DRE with chaperone; refer without waiting for FIT if a mass is found
FBC and ferritin; if FIT is low but symptoms persist and concern is strong, refer anyway (NICE HTG690)
safetyNet: Heavy bleeding, clots, faintness, severe pain or inability to pass anything → A&E
GP rings with the FIT result and sends any referral the same day; confirm the hospital appointment is received

SCA_LINKS.s: Visual algorithm · NICE NG12 FIT threshold

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by accepting the patient’s label. The history is easy to take if you ask the right two questions; the marks are lost when the cream goes out, the examination is skipped because the booking was remote, or the father’s death is never heard.

items.fail: Prescribing haemorrhoid cream because he has had piles before and asked for it.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Change in bowel habit and rectal bleeding at 50+ meet NICE HTG690 for FIT; a known benign diagnosis does not explain blood in the stool, altered habit and weight loss.
items.fix: Ask the discriminating questions — blood on the paper or mixed in, bowel habit, weight — then say plainly that cream is not the answer and why.

items.fail: Referring on symptoms alone without FIT, or quoting the old symptom-only suspected cancer referral criteria.
items.why: NICE NG12 makes FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g the referral trigger for most colorectal presentations; examiners expect the current pathway and the threshold stated.
items.fix: “The stool test decides the urgent referral — above 10 and you’re on the suspected cancer pathway. If I feel a lump on examination, I refer straight away.”

items.fail: Skipping the examination because the consultation is by video.
items.why: A rectal mass changes the pathway immediately, and GMC guidance expects an in-person assessment when remote care cannot meet the need.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face examination with a chaperone within a day or two, and explain exactly why it matters.

items.fail: Hearing “my dad had bowel cancer” and moving straight on to the plan.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The father’s death is the hidden agenda and the reason he is avoiding examination.
items.fix: Pause: “With your dad in mind, what’s been going through your head?” Then use his answer to shape the plan.

items.fail: Frightening him with “this could well be cancer” or overstating his inherited risk.
items.why: Catastrophising in a man already avoiding care risks disengagement; a single first-degree relative at 60 does not meet moderate-risk criteria (BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG 2019).
items.fix: Hold both truths: most bleeding is benign, and with these symptoms we check quickly.

items.fail: Ignoring the self-employed driver’s real constraints and offering a mid-morning slot next week.
items.why: A plan that does not fit his life will not happen — examiners mark whether the plan is tailored to the patient.
items.fix: Offer an early or late slot, FIT kit and bloods at the same visit, and hospital dates in advance.

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll let you know the results” and no named safety-net.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no owner for the result are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: “Heavy bleeding, faintness, bad pain or can’t pass anything — A&E. I’ll ring you with the FIT result myself.” Then teach-back.
